hints: Look closely at what X is actually joining. It links the pentagon (pentose sugar) of one nucleotide to the grey circle (phosphate) of the next nucleotide down the backbone.
Remember which bond makes the sugar-phosphate backbone of one polynucleotide strand, and contrast it with the bond that joins base to sugar and the bond that joins two strands together.
walkthrough:
**Read the diagram like a biologist**

Hi there, let's orient ourselves first. You can see a single chain with pentose sugars (pentagons), phosphates (grey circles) and nitrogenous bases A, G, U, C on the right. Bond X is on the left side, in the backbone.

Key observation: X is between nucleotides in the same strand, not between two strands.

**Apply the nucleic acid bonding rule**

In a polynucleotide, successive nucleotides are joined by a strong covalent bond between the phosphate of one nucleotide and the sugar of the next. This forms the sugar-phosphate backbone.

Rule to remember: sugar to phosphate along one strand = phosphodiester bond.

**Check and conclude**

X fits that description perfectly. It is not joining base to sugar, and it is not joining base to base across strands. So X must be the backbone linkage. That is the phosphodiester bond, option D.

options.A: Glycosidic bond joins the nitrogenous base to the pentose sugar (the horizontal line on the right), not sugar to phosphate along the backbone.
options.B: Hydrogen bonds hold two polynucleotide strands together between complementary bases, they do not join nucleotides in sequence along one strand like X.
options.C: Peptide bonds join amino acids together in proteins, they are never found in a nucleic acid molecule.
options.D: Correct. X links the sugar of one nucleotide to the phosphate of the next, forming the sugar-phosphate backbone. This is the phosphodiester bond.
